procedural_history.impugned_order: Order dated 06.04.2023 passed by the learned Single Judge of the High Court of Judicature at Rajasthan, Jaipur Bench in S.B. Criminal Miscellaneous 2nd Bail Application No.219 of 2023, granting bail to the respondents.
procedural_history.high_court_proceedings: The respondents filed Criminal Miscellaneous Bail Applications under Section 439 of the Cr.P.C. before the High Court of Judicature of Rajasthan. The High Court granted bail to the respondents on 06.04.2023, considering the statement of the prosecutrix and the possibility of trial taking time.
procedural_history.supreme_court_posture: The complainant, being aggrieved by the grant of bail by the High Court, preferred appeals by special leave to the Supreme Court, seeking cancellation of the bail. The State of Rajasthan's position is divided, supporting the complainant in one appeal and the accused in the other.

directions: The order of the High Court is set aside.
The accused/respondents shall surrender before the jurisdictional court within two weeks from the date of the order, failing which they shall be taken into custody.
The accused/respondents will be at liberty to seek bail after the evidence/depositions of the remaining witnesses are recorded.
In the event of such a bail application being filed, the High Court shall consider the same on its own merits and without being influenced by any of the observations made in this order.
The jurisdictional court shall not be influenced by any of the observations made in this order as they are limited to the present proceedings.

issue.issue_text: Whether the Single Judge of the High Court was justiﬁ ed in granting bail to the respondent-accused in connection with the FIR registered against them by the appellant-uncle of the minor girl alleging gang rape, threat of making video of rape recorded viral and extortion for the oﬀ ences punishable u/ss. 376D, 384, 506 IPC, s. 3 to 6 of POCSO Act, s. 3(2)(v) of the Scheduled Castes and Scheduled Tribes (Prevention of Atrocities) Act, 1989 and s. 66 of the Information Technology Act, 2000.

facts: The case involves an FIR filed by the uncle of a 15-year-old girl alleging she was gang-raped.
The accused were also charged with extortion and threatening to make a recorded video of the rape go viral.
The charges were filed under serious sections of the IPC (gang rape), POCSO Act, SC/ST Act, and the IT Act.
One of the accused is the son of a sitting MLA, and there was evidence suggesting tampering with evidence, such as missing hotel register entries and deleted CCTV footage.
The victim consistently reiterated the allegations in her statements to the police (S. 161 Cr.P.C.), the magistrate (S. 164 Cr.P.C.), and in her testimony before the court.
The High Court granted bail to the accused, primarily citing a 13-month delay in filing the FIR and the non-recovery of the alleged video.
law: The grant of bail is a discretionary power that must be exercised judiciously and not as a matter of course.

Courts considering bail must take into account several factors, including: the nature and gravity of the accusations, the severity of the potential punishment, the nature of the evidence, and any reasonable apprehension of witnesses being tampered with or threatened.
A delay in filing an FIR is not always fatal to the prosecution's case, especially when there are justifiable reasons for it, such as threats to the victim.
application: The Supreme Court found that the High Court had erred by being primarily swayed by the delay in filing the complaint and the non-recovery of the video.
The Court reasoned that the delay could be explained by the victim's young age, the constant threat of the video being made viral, and the influential status of one of the accused (the MLA's son).

The Supreme Court held that the High Court gave a "complete go by" to the substantial evidence against the accused. This included the serious allegations in the FIR and the consistent, unshattered testimony of the minor victim, which established a prima facie case.
The Court also noted the seriousness of the offenses, which carry a minimum sentence of 20 years to life, and the clear risk of evidence tampering, which the High Court failed to consider adequately.
The fact that the trial court had already framed charges indicated a prima facie case and reasonable suspicion of the accused's culpability, which should have weighed against granting bail.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court concluded that the High Court was not justified in granting bail. The High Court's order was found to be "bereft of material particulars" and failed to properly consider the gravity of the offense, the consistent testimony of the victim, the prima facie evidence, and the risk of tampering. Consequently, the Supreme Court set aside the High Court's order granting bail to the accused.

arguments.issue_text: Whether the Single Judge of the High Court was justiﬁ ed in granting bail to the respondent-accused in connection with the FIR registered against them by the appellant-uncle of the minor girl alleging gang rape, threat of making video of rape recorded viral and extortion for the oﬀ ences punishable u/ss. 376D, 384, 506 IPC, s. 3 to 6 of POCSO Act, s. 3(2)(v) of the Scheduled Castes and Scheduled Tribes (Prevention of Atrocities) Act, 1989 and s. 66 of the Information Technology Act, 2000.
appellant_arguments: The complainant, aggrieved by the grant of bail, appealed the High Court's order.
The prosecutrix has made clear allegations against the accused-respondents.
The State, in the case of one accused (Netram), supported the complainant's position and argued for the bail to be set aside.
respondent_arguments: There was a delay in lodging the FIR.
During the trial, the prosecution made admissions that revealed a 'hole in prosecution theory'.
The High Court correctly considered the statement of the prosecutrix recorded during the trial and the possibility of the trial being time-consuming when granting bail.
The State, in the case of another accused (Deepak), supported the defense and the material collected during the investigation.

ratio_decidendi.ratio: A superior court must intervene to set aside an order granting bail when there is prima facie material for a heinous offense and a likelihood that the accused will threaten witnesses or otherwise subvert the criminal justice system. The cancellation of bail requires cogent and overwhelming circumstances and cannot be done mechanically, with one of the primary considerations being the prima facie satisfaction of the court in support of the charge.
obiter: The offense alleged is an onslaught on the dignity of womanhood.
The age-old principle of ;= uk;ZLrq iwT;Urs jeUrs r= nsork% (where women are respected Gods live there) would recede to the background if the guilty are not punished by the process of law.

judicial_reasoning.core_finding: In cases involving heinous offenses that represent an onslaught on the dignity of womanhood, if there is prima facie material against the accused and a likelihood they could threaten or induce witnesses, a superior court must intervene to set aside an erroneous grant of bail to prevent the criminal justice system from being jettisoned.
legal_tests_applied: The factors to be borne in mind while considering an application for bail are: (i) whether there is any prima facie or reasonable ground to believe that the accused had committed the oﬀ ence; (ii) nature and gravity of the accusation; (iv) danger of the accused absconding or ﬂ eeing, if released on bail; (vii) reasonable apprehension of the witnesses being inﬂ uenced; and (viii) danger, of course, of justice being thwarted by grant of bail.
There ought to be always a prima facie satisfaction of the Court in support of the charge.

It is incumbent upon the High Court to exercise its discretion judiciously, cautiously and strictly in compliance with the basic principles laid down in a plethora of decisions of this Court on the point.
why_respondent_won: The offence alleged is heinous and an onslaught on the dignity of womanhood, and allowing the accused to move freely in society despite prima facie material creates a risk of them threatening or inducing prosecution witnesses.

Allowing accused persons in such serious cases to be free before guilt is proven, where they are likely to interfere with witnesses, would 'jettison the criminal justice system', necessitating intervention by a superior court to undo the damage from the erroneous bail order.
The High Court's order granting bail was erroneous, requiring it to be set aside.
policy_considerations: The Courts have placed the liberty of an individual at a high pedestal and extended the protection to such rights whenever and wherever required. In the same breadth, it requires to be noticed that emphasis has also been laid on furnishing reasons for granting bail while balancing it with the requirement of a fair trial.

The age old principle of ;= uk;ZLrq iwT;Urs jeUrs r= nsork% (where women are respected Gods live there) would recede to the background if the guilty are not punished by process of law or accused persons are allowed to move around freely in the society despite prima facie material.
It is a heinous crime against the society and as such the court ought to be rather circumspect and cautious in its approach in a matter which stands out to be a social crime of a very serious nature.
